clue.text: Plain diamond in striking clasp

indicators.note: the diamond sits inside the other word, so 'in' signals one piece placed within another
the outer word holds the gem as a clasp grips a stone, confirming the container reading

parts.note: something striking is notable, worth remarking on
ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: A simple diamond set in an eye-catching clasp, a piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like an adjective describing the diamond, but it is the definition, in its sense of obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: Something plain in the sense of clear and obvious is easily seen or perceived.

clue.text: Non-playing coach attached to cricket side

parts.note: the off side is one half of a cricket field, the side the batsman faces
a stagecoach, or stage, is a horse-drawn coach

explanation.surface: A coach who does not play is attached to a cricket team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' reads as a trainer, but here it is the old horse-drawn stage; 'side' is not a team but the off side of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who is not on stage at the moment is not playing, out of sight in the wings.

clue.text: Lose this and you won't finish the yarn

definitions.text: Lose this and you won't finish the yarn

parts.words: Lose this and you won't finish the yarn
parts.note: a yarn is both a spun strand for knitting and a long story; losing your place in either stops you finishing

explanation.surface: A warning that a knitter who drops something will never complete the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing the line of a story, its connecting strand, means a storyteller cannot finish the tale.

clue.text: Work to furrow the brow

definitions.meaning: to work with needles and wool, making a jumper
to ... the brows is to draw them together in a frown

explanation.definitionFit: Knitting is a kind of craft work, and one knits one's brows when frowning, both senses of the same verb.

clue.text: Tourists may go to see something cheekily displayed by ladies

definitions.meaning: a scenic place that visitors travel to admire
a small dark mark on the cheek, once painted on by fashionable women

explanation.definitionFit: A scenic attraction and a decorative mole or patch share the same two-word name.

clue.text: End union trouble with suggestion

indicators.note: to trouble is to stir up or disturb, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A strike is ended with a hint dropped to the trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges the letters of END UNION; 'with' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An innuendo is an indirect hint or insinuation, a sly suggestion rather than a plain statement.

clue.text: Stop vehicle and issue a reprimand

definitions.meaning: a driver pulls up when bringing a car to a halt
to pull someone up is to tell them off for a fault

explanation.definitionFit: Halting a car and checking someone for a mistake are both expressed by the same phrasal verb.

clue.text: Depend on entirely? Not half!

indicators.note: not the first half of the word, so only its second four letters remain

explanation.surface: A person is asked whether they rely on someone completely and answers with emphatic agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it tells you to drop the first half of ENTIRELY.
explanation.definitionFit: To rely on someone is to depend on them, trusting them to come through.

clue.text: Slight possibility of being caught at cover?

definitions.meaning: a remote likelihood that something might happen
a catching chance offered to the cover fielder, cover being a fielding position on the off side in cricket

explanation.definitionFit: A long shot is a slim possibility, and in cricket a catch at cover would be a chance on the off side.

clue.text: Hopeless, lacking purpose

definitions.meaning: having no function, serving no end

explanation.definitionFit: Something futile is hopeless and pointless, without any value or function.

clue.text: Vet gets bug out of parrot's head

indicators.note: the creature gets, that is takes in, the extra letter

parts.note: a bug is an insect

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A vet removes a parasite from a parrot's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vet' looks like the animal doctor, but it is the verb meaning examine; 'out of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To vet something is to examine it carefully, check it over before approval.

clue.text: American friend seen around university most of the time

parts.note: US is short for United States, so American
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: An American pal is regularly seen about the campus.
explanation.definitionFit: Usually means normally or as a rule, true on most occasions.

clue.text: Animal not usually laden

indicators.note: not in the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A beast that is rarely loaded with burdens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not usually' looks like a statement about loads but signals a rearrangement of LADEN.
explanation.definitionFit: The eland is a large African antelope, a type of animal.

clue.text: There's worse to come out of this

definitions.text: There's worse to come out of this

parts.words: There's worse to come out of this
parts.note: the saying 'out of the ___ into the fire' warns that escaping one trouble lands you in worse

explanation.surface: A gloomy warning that things will only get worse after this.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb names this kitchen utensil as the lesser danger, escaped only into the fire.

clue.text: Italian girl showing cleavage in England's capital

parts.note: Flo is a girl's name, short for Florence
a rent is a split or tear, a cleaving

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An Italian girl reveals a low neckline in London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'England's capital' is not London but the letter E; 'cleavage' is a split, not a neckline.
explanation.definitionFit: A Florentine is a native of Florence, so an Italian of that city.

clue.text: Nags drunken tinker for no good reason

parts.note: to needle someone is to nag or goad them
Christopher Sly is the drunken tinker in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew

explanation.surface: A woman keeps on at a drunken mender of pots for no good reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunken' looks like an anagram signal, but 'drunken tinker' is Christopher Sly, the drunk in the framing story of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Needlessly means without necessity, with no good reason.

clue.text: Action following disastrous engagement?

parts.note: an engagement here is a promise to marry, and an action is a lawsuit brought when it is broken off

explanation.surface: Military action after a failed battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A suit for jilting was once brought by a fiance abandoned after agreeing to marry.

clue.text: A stone pitcher

parts.note: not a jug made of stone, but something that pitches, that is throws, stones

explanation.surface: An earthenware jug.
explanation.definitionFit: A slingshot is a device for hurling small stones, so it pitches them.

clue.text: Sacked, no doubt

definitions.meaning: put into a sack, literally in a bag
certain to be achieved, as good as secured

explanation.definitionFit: Something bagged is literally inside a bag, and figuratively a done deal, assured.

clue.text: A law to punish backward people in a race

indicators.note: the word for punishing is read from right to left

parts.note: to cane is to punish with a stick

indicators.note: the people go inside the race

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
men means people

explanation.surface: A law passed to punish slow runners in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' looks like a description of slow people, but it reverses the punishing word; 'in' puts the people inside the TT, the Isle of Man motorcycle race. 'A law' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An enactment is a law that has been passed by a legislature.

clue.text: A vote having gone to the other side

definitions.text: having gone to the other side

parts.note: a voter marks a ballot with a cross

explanation.surface: A ballot cast by someone who has defected.
explanation.definitionFit: Across means over to the far side, having crossed.

clue.text: Former tax reduced by a pound — celebrate!

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: the tax word is made smaller by losing one letter

parts.note: a toll is a charge or tax for using a road or bridge
L stands for pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: Celebrate: an old levy has been cut by a pound!
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise highly, to celebrate someone's merits.

clue.text: Time conceals deserter's mistakes

indicators.note: the time word hides the other inside it

parts.note: an era is a period of time
a rat is someone who deserts, as rats leave a sinking ship

explanation.surface: Over time, a deserter's errors are covered up.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'deserter's' gives no letter; the mistakes are not the deserter's at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are a list of errors, mistakes noted in a printed book.

clue.text: Defence provided by a regimental mascot

parts.note: the Paras are the Parachute Regiment of the British Army
a regimental mascot is often an animal, a pet

explanation.surface: A goat or dog kept by the regiment offers protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' is a link word: a Para's pet would be a regimental mascot.
explanation.definitionFit: A parapet is a low protective wall on a rampart, a defensive barrier.

clue.text: Look what we do with the Joneses!

indicators.note: the idiom completes as 'keep up with the Joneses', and in a down light 'up' reverses

parts.note: what we try to do with the neighbours is keep up

explanation.surface: Peer at what we do to keep up with the neighbours!
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'keeping up with the Joneses' supplies the 'up', which in a down answer turns KEEP to read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To peek is to take a quick look, a sly glance.

clue.text: Footnote to army group involved in operations

indicators.note: the note is attached to the end of the army word

parts.note: a force is a body of troops
PS, postscript, is a note added at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A footnote to an army unit's part in military operations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'operations' sounds military but refers to surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: Forceps are surgical tongs, instruments used in operations.

clue.text: Obscure-sounding round-the-world traveller

indicators.note: the answer sounds like a word meaning obscure when spoken

parts.note: to fog is to obscure or cloud

explanation.surface: A globetrotter whose name sounds unclear.
explanation.walkthrough: Phileas Fogg travels round the world in Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days.
explanation.definitionFit: Phileas Fogg is Jules Verne's hero who circles the globe in eighty days.

clue.text: Moderate money providing support for teacher

parts.note: to ease is to moderate or lessen
L stands for pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: Moderate pay offers some support for a teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' looks like money for a teacher, but it is the stand holding a blackboard.
explanation.definitionFit: An easel is a stand that holds a blackboard or picture, supporting it for a teacher.

clue.text: Dark autumn evening

parts.note: night is the dark part of the day
fall is the American word for autumn

explanation.surface: A dark evening in the autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark autumn evening' reads as one picture; only 'evening' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightfall is dusk, the start of night at the close of the evening.
